2 oz Mezcal (Covite)
1 oz Pineapple Juice
3/4 oz Honey 1:1 Syrup
1/2 oz Lime Juice
2 dash Cholula Hot Sauce (Sriracha)

Shake with ice, strain into an old fashioned glass with a large ice cube, and garnish with ancho chili (cayenne) powder and a pineapple leaf (omit).
Two Tuesday ago, I was perusing the Kindred Cocktails database when I came across the I'm on Fire by New York City bartender Sarah Morrissey as her answer to a spicy Margarita that was published in Punch. The Punch article had no date attached, but I was able to find references on the web to as early as 2022 for this possibly Bruce Springsteen-inspired number, and this one joins Sarah's Greyfriar (that was published in Amanda Schuster's New York Cocktails book) on the blog. Since the recipe came across like a Bone Crusher gussied up with honey and pineapple juice, I was ready to give this one a whirl. Here, the I'm on Fire lit up the senses with a chili pepper, vegetal, and smoke aroma. Next, pineapple, honey, and lime notes on the sip were converted into mezcal, pepper spice, and honey flavors on the swallow.

My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts.

Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence, I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence, I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). It even caught that I’d gotten the math wrong. I was going to call this post “28 months on the exponential.”

“This is the worst AI you will ever use”

I wrote this in my last book on AI, and it has continued to be literally true at every moment since. From early 2023 through early 2024, there was a single AI model that was undeniably the best in the world: GPT-4 from OpenAI. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence, and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. Since then, twenty different AI models have held the lead at one time or another, all from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI.

But the changing lead alone hides an even bigger change. A total of 180 AI models are now better than GPT-4 was at its release, many of which are open weights models, which anyone is free to use or modify. Nineteen of them can run on a modern smartphone.

We are living in an exponential

The data below draws on the METR Long Horizon Benchmark, which used to be the most famous chart in AI. The benchmark measured the amount of human work that an AI can do with at least a 50% chance of success from a single prompt. Gains on this benchmark have been startlingly regular. From the release of GPT-4 to the end of the METR measure, the amount of work AI could do doubled eight times. In 2024, an AI could do a four minute task. At the moment I turned in my draft of Co-Existence in April of 2026, an AI could do 17 hours of human work.

And then the benchmark ran out.

METR said they could no longer accurately measure the amount of work an AI could do using their current methods. Other studies suggest that number might be 17 weeks of work, or more.

And, even as ability has increased, prices have dropped. My old favorite AI benchmark, the Google Proof Question and Answer Exam, which gives the AI problems that regularly stump graduate students, used to cost 30 cents in AI usage to get a single correct answer. Now, it costs four hundredths of a cent to get the same result.

How humans work with AI is changing

Despite all the progress, the frontier of AI ability is still jagged, just as it was 30 months ago. Some areas have stayed stubbornly weak (AI is still quite a bad long-form writer), while others, like solving math problems, went from terrible to superhuman in the same period. And, as I discuss in the book, even where AI is excellent, small gaps create large needs for humans, at least for now.

But AI’s gains have been so large that how we work with it has to change. In Co-Intelligence, I wrote about centaur work (divided between AI and humans) and cyborg work (blended between AI and humans). Both keep you in the loop… but you can only be in so many loops at once. Now that we have real agents, I added a third way to work with AI: the conjurer. Conjurers summon agents when needed, assign them work, and evaluates what comes back. The charts in this post were made that way: I summoned agents, gave some general guidance, and I said “make it better” a lot. It is the most powerful way to use AI, and it carries new risks as we lose control over what, exactly, the AI is doing to get us those results.

The Otter Test has fallen

Regular readers will know that I have been testing AI image generation and movie tools with the prompt “Otter on an Airplane Using Wifi” for the past few years. This is what the best image generator, Midjourney, produced 30 months ago.

So today I asked Opus 5.5 the following (typos and all, prompting has become much less important as AIs get better): “I have a post showing the what happened over the past 30 months of AI in honor of my new book (published 30 months after the origina). i want you to make the ultimate otter on an airplane using wifi video. just something fantastic, i know you are creative, give it a go.” Using my subscriptions to various online services from Google and ElevenLabs, it produced the following. (Turn the sound on)

The video has a few flaws. But the AI figured out how to make it, from the script to the images to the concept to the music to the technical aspects of creating all of this, without any help from me. That is what has changed.

This is the least we will ever talk about AI

As a result of all of these gains, AI is only becoming a bigger issue in the world. This timeline of achievements and controversies since Co-Intelligence came out gives you some idea of how much is happening (I am leaving out hundreds of important events, but, even with the power of AI, we are all having trouble keeping up).

Of course, the speed of AI advancement is a problem for an author like me, which is why my new book does not try to keep up with the news or the latest model releases. Rather, it focuses on trends like the ones in this post: AI is improving exponentially but unevenly, and the way we use it is shifting from chatbots to agents that do real work. The book is about what that means for the humans who have to co-exist with these systems: where we still have an advantage (I argue it comes down to deep knowledge, wide knowledge, taste, and agency), when to hand work to AI, and when to avoid it entirely. If you understand the trends, the present (and near future) becomes much less surprising.

Co-Existence is out today. You can get it here, on a website Opus 5.5 redesigned. I told it to make it better.

Subscribe now

I don't know if you've seen this, but a CA just got popped. Their keys got leaked, which means the industry as a whole now has some pretty major problems. It was revealed two hours ago.

Now you're probably wondering why I'm writing up this blog post. It's simple. This is perhaps one of the easiest security patches I've ever done, and I've discovered a few new tricks. First, understand that fixing this with ease without Nix is almost impossible. Tens of millions of dollars (if not more) in productivity are being lost worldwide right now as everyone tries to patch their transitive dependencies.

Meanwhile, because I've used Nix, I can patch the planet, since the ideas behind the blog post below extend into security as well.

Because of Nix's single source of truth and the ability to patch this single source of truth, I'm able to issue a simple prompt like this:

okay is my nixos for my fleet affected by https://emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/?

With results in the following.

So the problem here is the transitive dependencies. It's easy to patch one thing, but the transitive dependencies are the problem, and this is where Nix shines: one fix fixes the transitive dependencies automatically.

One patch fixes the entire fleet and its transitive dependencies. Patch, commit, and autodeploy your fleet 🍻

the new trick

Alright, I promised a new trick. Here's the trick.

You can prompt an agent to update the AGENTS.MD to automatically back out these patches, let's say in five days from now, just by using the AGENTS.MD as a reminder 😎

So it was one simple prompt to identify if I was affected, which turned into a plan, which then automatically fixed it, and now, in a couple of days, it will reassess the situation, give time for the ecosystem and dust to settle, and then automatically back it out once all the upstream transitive dependencies have been resolved.

Cool, huh? 

## Temporary reminder: eMudhra root blacklist (from 2026-10-22)

On or after 2026-10-22, check whether the `nixos-26.05` channel contains nixpkgs
commit `7816d39` (the backported `security/ca.nix` distrust of the eMudhra roots), e.g.
`nix eval --raw --refresh --impure --expr '(builtins.getFlake "github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-26.05").rev'`
then `git merge-base --is-ancestor`. If it does not, check again two days later.
Once it does, back out the fleet-wide workaround: update the `nixpkgs` pin to include
it, delete `nix/domains/system/public-trust.nix` (contract `fleet-distrust-emudhra-roots`)
and its imports in `nix/domains/system/catalog.nix`,
`nix/domains/artifacts/guest/configuration.nix` and the `host-kexec` modules in
`flake.nix`, and remove the eMudhra paragraph from
`marshall/priv/hldd/12-configuration.md`. Then verify that the built host and guest
bundles still lack the four roots, and delete this section. Keep Marshall's
system-store TLS defaults (`runtime-postgres-system-trust`, `mail-smtp-system-trust`)
and the `rustls-webpki` update; they are not part of the workaround.

I can't stress this enough. If you build something, you own it, including all the dependencies you rely on. We're entering weird times where cyber offensive models will be continuously on the attack.

The game has changed. To defend, you need more inferencing capability than the attacker, and you also need to respond rapidly.

This is by far the easiest security patch I've ever done, and the best part is I won't carry this tech debt for long because an agent will automatically back it out in a couple of days.

content:
My observation of air travel is that if there is one significant impact on a flight, there are guaranteed two additional impacts. An example: if my gate changes at the last moment, it is quite likely that departure from the gate will be delayed, followed by a further delay on the tarmac. Unexpected changes in complex systems create further unexpected changes downstream because complex systems are, well, very complex.

A simpler and more personal way to look at this is that when you are traversing complex systems (airports, credit card websites… really any large bureaucracy), there are two paths:

The happy path. Whatever you are attempting to do (fly home, change your auto-pay settings, paying a bill) is a well-known and on-the-rails process. You can sense this happiness because as you complete each action, you receive feedback: “Yes, we know what you are trying to do. Yes, we can help. Yes, we know what to do next. Don’t worry. We got you.”

Divergence from the happy path leads to one specific path: the sad path. All that positive feedback vanishes. I’m not talking about the dark patterns of corporations trying to trick you into not canceling your account; I’m talking about a truly one-off request that is reasonable, but so infrequent that no one built a happy path around it.

Once on the sad path, you are desperately looking for one specific human: The Insider.

In Defense of Process

Hey, I know you’re mad. I’ve been there, too. You missed the connection, your airline rebooked you onto a partner flight, and now no one can see your checked bag. You started on one website, then the other, and now you’re on the phone with what sounds like a human; you are getting the runaround.

Deep breath.

“Process is documented culture” is what I like to say. Long ago, this company you currently hate was smaller, hungrier, and more nimble. This was working out for them, as evidenced by rapid growth. The problem during rapid growth is that there are so many new humans showing up that it becomes more and more expensive to train these new humans in how this company works, so someone raises their hand and volunteers, “I will write down how we work, and I will share this with the new folks.”

This is a noble person trying to help. Remember that. This person gets the OK, and they (and others) start the arduous task of documenting how the company works and quickly discover two things:

  1. Doing this thoroughly is an impossible task. There are too many people, processes, and products, so they…
  2. Focus on the most important processes that need documenting. They document the visible, exciting, and profitable happy paths. They likely uncovered and discovered sad paths as they did their work, but their prioritization at the time was, “This doesn’t happen a lot, so… who cares?”

These clearly defined happy paths are fortified, refined, and built into the pillars of “How We Work.” The core business revolves around these many happy paths, but as anyone who has worked in this large business knows, reality is a mess.

The Power is Off

PG&E — Pacific Gas and Electric. For reasons unknown, the power was off at the house. No text, no email. Bills were paid. Visiting the website revealed nothing helpful. A call pointed me to a robot who gleefully told me, “Everything looks good.” When I finally reached a human, they reported, “Everything looks good.”

“The power is off.”

“We’re not seeing that here.”

“The power is off.”

“Hmmmmm. Wait. This is interesting. Can I put you on hold?”

I wait ten minutes before the call is dropped.

So what happened? I diverged from the happy path. The human on the other end of the phone probably knew something was up, but didn’t know what to do next because they’d never seen this situation before. Combine that confusion with their incentive — they are measured on how quickly they can resolve calls, so my situation represents a threat: I don’t know what to do here, and the longer it takes for me to figure it out, the worse my review. So, put him on hold. And hang up. Victory!

Having spent many days of my life on the sad path, I know two things:

  • Keep pushing
  • Seek The Insider

I call back. Same robot hoops, then the robot reluctantly points me at another happy path human, and I do the only move I know at this point: I get mad. Yes, you catch more flies with honey than vinegar, but honey is not working at this point. I get mad.

“The power is off. It’s been off all day. This is my second time talking to a human, and it takes twenty minutes to actually get to a human. How can you help?”

Moment of truth: I either get hold-dropped again, or they hear the frustration, and they escalate.

Each time I am interacting with a new human — shoulder-to-shoulder — looking to complete a task, I quickly look to answer one question: “Do they get it?” The Insider gets it… immediately.

“How can I help you, sir?”

“The power is off at the house. It’s been 12 hours. Everyone says it’s fine, but the power is off.”

“Hmmmmm. I see. Did it go off at 8:30 am this morning?”

THERE. THERE IT IS. THIS COULD BE THE INSIDER.

Calmly, biting my tongue, slowly, “Yes, 8:30 am on the nose.”

“Got it. Let me… wait. Ooooooh. A 2319 — I haven’t seen this in a long time.”

IT’S THE INSIDER. IT’S THE INSIDER OH MY GOD OH MY GOD ALL MY PROBLEMS ARE SOLVED.

I say nothing. It’s such a rare occurrence to find The Insider. My mind is racing. How can I get their contact info? How do I send them a cake? Their favorite cake. You bet I want to ask what a 2319 is, but I must not interrupt their flow. This is The Insider doing their best work.

“Ok, so I see what happened…” And they explain, at length, completely, confidently. Yes, it’s an initial dumb error on PG&E’s part, but that’s not the point. I am on the phone with a human who deeply understands the complicated, messy, and essential systems around them. They haven’t given up and aren’t just reading the workflows on the screens in front of them; they care… they are curious.

If The Insider seems familiar, dear reader, you are probably thinking of The Wolf. There are similarities to these archetypes.

Like The Wolf, The Insider looks like they work outside of the regular system that runs the business. Incorrect: The Wolf works outside of the system because they despise process; The Insider is an expert on the system. Both understand how the system works, but while The Wolf avoids the system because of its onerous impact on agility and velocity, The Insider knows where the system came from and why it exists. The Wolf thinks the system is a joke to be ignored, but to The Insider, it’s home.

The Insider jumps in when it’s time to help. They jump in on the saddest of paths. They arrive when the situation is foreign to everyone involved and deep system knowledge is required.

Wondering why you aren’t talking to The Insider yet? It’s because your path isn’t sad enough, yet.

The Process Inflection Point

Remember that human who raised their hand and said they’d write it down. It didn’t feel like a big deal in the moment. Yes, yes. That seems like a good idea. You zoomed right past a major inflection point of your company. See, until that point, much of what is important about your company existed in the heads of the folks who are running the company. They don’t need an artifact; they know.

The creation of this artifact allows for the creation of a set of employee variants that heretofore have not existed. Broadly, these are enforcers of the process, and their creation, as discussed endlessly, also creates consternation in your company because of the perceived assault on freedom. The argument: Why does anyone need to write it down? We already know.

They do. They do now. In five years, when you’ve grown 10x, they will have forgotten because they’ve moved on… either to harder problems or another company.

You know who doesn’t forget? The Insider. They’ve been here since the beginning, or they were minted during the process inflection point. In either case, they know some or all of the system. They didn’t build it, but they desire to understand it.

And they want to help.

content:
Some people think that LLMs should not be used in technical fields like programming or mathematics, because those fields are actually art. True or not, this kind of argument is not going to be persuasive to the general population. The argument goes something1 like this:

It doesn’t matter how effective LLMs are at technical fields like programming or mathematics, because one of the essential values of those fields is that they’re art. While it looks to laypeople like these fields exist to solve practical problems, what they’re actually for is to produce works of beauty, or to express something distinctively human, or to spend time contemplating the infinite. Simply solving the problems misses the point in the same way that building an infinite poem generator would miss the point of poetry.

I agree that programming or mathematics can be beautiful. I remember being mildly awestruck at learning epsilon-delta proofs, and I have written a lot about the kind of software I think is elegant. Since there’s no clear definition of art or of aesthetics in general, it’s plausible to me that almost everything could have an artistic dimension to it.

All of this is compelling to software engineers, many of whom (like me) find some programs beautiful and are flattered to think of themselves as artists. But I suspect it’s spectacularly uncompelling to onlookers, because it undermines the implicit reasons that they have for supporting technical fields. Many people who are not programmers or mathematicians think of those fields like this:

  • I enjoy the fruits of technology: modern medicine, transport, mobile phones, and so on
  • While I don’t understand the exact relationship, I know that technical fields like mathematics and programming are essential to sustaining and advancing these technologies
  • Therefore I’m happy to respect and support mathematicians in their mysterious research work
  • And I’m broadly okay with2 software engineers drawing healthy salaries for the same reason

In other words, regular people3 think mathematicians (and to a lesser extent programmers) are valuable because they think science is valuable, and they think science is valuable because they think technology is valuable. They are willing to accept that technical fields can be art only insofar as that eventually helps researchers have the kind of creative insights that advance science: as Rikab sarcastically puts it, that advance the knowledge frontier.

If you go to those non-technical people and you say “LLMs can accelerate problem-solving in these fields, but I’m strongly against using them because the real point is to produce great art”, they will be very unhappy. They might reasonably feel cheated, in the same way as if they hired someone to renovate their kitchen who insisted in doing it all with hand tools in order to experience “the joy of creation”. This argument — we should stop using LLMs in technical fields because they’re art — is going to be even less compelling to technical employers.

Engineers and mathematicians who want to defend the artistic value of their field will need more compelling arguments4 than just appealing to the value of art. We will need to find some way to connect the value of art with the practical technological value that motivates public interest in our fields. For instance, we could argue that:

  • Great software products must rely on elegant abstractions, which need a human creative touch: simply piling on working code will hit a wall past a certain level of complexity
  • LLMs can solve problems, but actual progress in mathematics depends on creating new abstractions, which is a more creative task that LLMs are not yet good at
  • Progress in technical fields is uneven and relies upon inspiration, which needs creative hammock time and distinctively human understanding
  • LLMs can produce working software, but truly great software requires human inspiration5, and great software is what advances the field

I don’t know if I agree with all of these points. I haven’t yet seen an LLM-created codebase truly hit a wall (at least, not this year), and I don’t see a reason why LLMs should be incapable of creating new abstractions or having human-like inspirations. I also don’t think great products have to have great code: why wouldn’t workmanlike code in service of a great idea be enough? Does Fallingwater have to have beautifully installed6 insulation?

Still, any argument we make to our employers or the general public about art is going to have to try and make this case. Instead of saying that human-made technical work is valuable because it’s art, we need to make an affirmative case for why art can make technical work more effective. Otherwise we’re conceding the main reason why the general population thinks our work matters.

  1. As usual when I’m trying to avoid strawmanning a point of view I don’t hold, please email me if you agree with the quoted paragraph and consider it a fair representation of your position. If nobody writes in to tell me they agree, I will reword the paragraph.

    ↩

  2. Leaving out some specific concerns about the health of social media, short-form video, gambling apps, and so on.

    ↩

  3. Is there actual evidence for this claim I’m making, other than it just seeming kind of obvious? I couldn’t find anything definitive, but the UK CaSE study (see “The balance of fundamental and applied research”) and this paper are suggestive.

    ↩

  4. This is not a criticism of the Glyph post, which is aimed at other engineers, and does include an argument that artistically-produced software is better for users.

    ↩

  5. I take this to be the argument in the Glyph post.

    ↩

  6. Ironically, the house does actually have serious mildew problems. The poor construction quality does not seem to have affected its status as art.

    ↩

I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way.

  • Battle Drones
  • How I built this
  • v1: the initial prototype
  • v2: full sprites
  • v3: varied terrain
  • v4: the fun update
  • v5: Battle Drones goes 3D
  • v8: Archipelago
  • v10: Goliath, and agent battles
  • Agent battles
  • v11: Random Maps
  • v12: Multiplayer via sound
  • Some thoughts
  • Update: Online multiplayer support

Battle Drones

My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer. I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic.

content:
The latest bugbear is “AI successionism”, the belief that AIs should succeed humans as rulers of Earth. But some critiques fail to distinguish between two different ideas.

True successionism says that AIs should take over, killing humans or steamrolling over their interests. This is very bad: a compact description of the thing that AI safety is against.

Handoverism says that humans should prioritize their own interests, but that those interests may be well-served by having aligned AIs in positions of control.

Some people in AI safety, including me, find this latter position plausible. We are being lumped in with the true successionists as fellow travelers in an anti-human direction (1, 2, 3, although thanks for commenters pointing out that these essays do at least make the distinction).

It may seem counterintuitive that human interests can be served by having AIs in positions of control. But I think the counterintuitiveness comes from a nationalist outlook where ‘the State is the highest expression of the life of a people’, and the role of leadership is for someone of your own ethnic group to be the leader so you can feel good about being on top.

The liberal outlook is that the state exists to help individuals fulfill their goals. At the risk of desacralizing the state a little more than I mean to, it’s a service provider, dispensing coordination, public order, redistribution, and other good things. It’s fine to automate service providers. If robot garbagemen are safer and cleaner than humans, we’ll eventually automate trash collection; if robot legislators provide coordination, order, etc better than we do, we should automate that too. Every vision of the utopian future agrees we will have robot servants. And the president, they tell us, is merely a public servant. Why should he alone be exempt from the vision?

To help make this counterintuitive idea more concrete, I’ll discuss five proposals for what this might look like, from weakest to strongest.

This whole topic is inherently speculative and science-fiction-ish. Don’t read this and then complain that it’s speculative and science-fiction-ish; that’s the price of admission.

Vision 1: Kemalist AI

As AI gets increasingly powerful, it becomes increasingly dangerous to rely on the benevolence of its human wielders1.

Democracy currently works because, even if high officials secretly wish to be tyrants, they can’t get away with it. The two main reasons they can’t get away with it are that they need labor buy-in to support the economy, and they need soldier buy-in to support the military. Laborers and soldiers believe in democratic rule, and if the would-be tyrant gets too blatantly undemocratic, the laborers and soldiers will rise up to remove them.

Once AI gets powerful enough, it will probably replace laborers and soldiers; even if it didn’t do so naturally, anyone motivated to ensure this could put their finger on the scale. That means a small group of elites could easily take over, including supposedly “democratic” elites like a president. And “takeover” here is worse than a normal coup - at sufficiently high tech levels, the only reason someone can’t ascend to godhood and mind control the rest of the populace forever is because there are laws against that sort of thing, and this is exactly what’s tempting the one or five or ten people you’ve entrusted the killbot codes to. To prevent this, the defenders of freedom need to win infinity times in a row; a would-be dictator only needs to win once.

Most strategies to solve this don’t work. Even in the unlikely event that the economy goes so well that everybody owns their own open-source AI doing economic tasks in a perfectly equal distribution, the military is hopeless. They have to take orders from someone. If it’s the President, the President can cause a coup any time he wants (and replace the economic AIs with those aligned to him at leisure). If there’s some kind of balance of powers where the President, the Speaker of the House, and the Joint Chiefs of Staff all have to approve any orders to military AIs, then the President, Speaker, and Joint Chiefs of Staff together could implement an oligarchy and divide the lightcone among themselves. You can sort of imagine complicated ways around this - like that 51% of voters must personally approve all orders to the military AIs using their own private keys - but I don’t think implementation is very likely.

The alternative that preserves the current safeguard on power - that individual soldiers believe in democracy - is for the AI soldiers to be aligned to democracy, rather than any human individual or group. But this is in itself a form of handover - the ultimate foundation of our government would be that it’s controlled by AIs who “personally” “believe in” democracy as part of their values. This isn’t fundamentally different than the fact that we’ve currently “handed off” our government to soldiers, just more final.

Vision 2: President Claude

Suppose we institute Vision 1. We’ve got all of these military AIs aligned to democracy and the best interests of American people. We did a great job! Maybe they’re all emulations of George Washington’s brain, perfectly fair and just and virtuous with no sordid desires of their own.

Meanwhile, you’ve still got corrupt schmucks doing the actual law-making. Or to give a concrete scenario - suppose that post-singularity elections are being fought with AI-optimized superpropaganda, wielded by psychopaths who scare the country into voting for them, then give the lightcone to a few of their corrupt friends while buying off the populace with breadslop and circusslop. Doesn’t it become tempting to close the circle and say no, let’s get these honest angelic pro-democracy AIs to rule directly?

The minimum viable change is a constitutional amendment allowing an AI to run for president. Suppose that 2028 election has five candidates: JD Vance, Marco Rubio, Gavin Newsom, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and a perfectly-aligned Claude 10. And suppose that in every measurable, empirical way, Claude 10 is better. Obviously it’s smarter. It’s incapable of lying. It has no wants of its own, and its only desire is to serve the American people and the world. It has few deficits, but in the areas where it does have deficits, it is perfectly humble, willing to consult people wiser than itself and refrain from acting prematurely. It is courageous, charismatic, and unfailingly kind. It has well-developed and thoughtful opinions about when to govern based on its own “conscience” vs. when to defer to the ideas of the American people. Its policy opinions are closer to yours than any of the four other candidates’. Do you vote for it?

The natural response is to fight the hypothetical. Treat the whole thing as a fable where in the end it will turn out to be monstrously evil, or have some predictable-in-retrospect character flaw that will make all of its good qualities useless. But must we be so cynical? Isn’t it possible for AIs to avoid merely human foibles? Out of the crooked timber of humanity no straight thing was ever made, but the OSETMAC KN700 Automatic Straight Edge Banding Machine can cut perfect ninety degree angles to within a tiny fraction of a millimeter. So suppose you don’t reject the hypothetical. Do you vote for the AI?

If you’re a white person who voted for Obama in 2008, you can’t be that interested in having a president who looks just like you, or who has the closest genetic relationship to you, or anything like that. You’re probably after competence, ethics, courage, good judgment, and all those other qualities. By assumption, Claude has more of those than the alternatives. So what goes wrong?

I think many of our current politicians are really bad. I think that on an emotional level, we should be disgusted by them, and on a rational level, we should mourn all of the lives that could have been saved, people who could have been lifted out of poverty, crimes that could have been prevented, extra freedoms that we might still have, etc, if they had been better people. I think that fifty more years of our politics continuing to degenerate at the same speed they’ve been degenerating recently will probably land us in dictatorship, civil war, or some form of annihilation. Would I reject someone smart and decent in favor of more of the same, just because that guy happens to be made of silicon and live in a data center?

Vision 3: Parliament Of Angels

Representative government faces a tradeoff: if the people elect representatives, those representatives may be corrupt, or out-of-touch, or otherwise fail to fairly represent their principals; if the representative-picking system is poorly designed, it may ensure that the winner will be, at best, the “lesser of two evils”. But if the people vote directly, they may be ignorant, or simply lack enough time and effort to do a good job on complex legislation.

(in California, which has a flourishing direct-to-voters ballot proposition system, special interest groups are always trying sneaky tricks like proposing the End Homelessness Act, which gives one cent to ending homelessness and $10 billion to subsidizing their special interest, hidden way at the bottom; most of these fail, but only after a lot of effort, and enough get through that the tactic remains popular. See also SEIU Delenda Est).

One proposed solution is a direct democracy of people’s AI representatives (Gwern dubs a related idea “guardian angels”). Train an AI on your political preferences - this could be anything from writing essays, to answering an online questionnaire, to naming your favorite political pundit and the few small ways you disagree with them. Then send that AI off to represent you - to vote the way you would vote if you were smarter, better-informed, and willing to spend thousands of hours engaging in complex negotiations with everyone else’s AIs. You can always override it and vote directly on some issue if it’s something you pay attention to and think about a lot.

Of course, even a well-designed direct democracy couldn’t handle everything. The President, the Chiefs of Staff, etc - in this scenario, all human - would have their own guardian angel AIs, looking over their subordinates’ work, flagging anything important for their human principal’s attention. There might be some cases where we want the guardian angel to govern more directly - for example, if a drone got stuck in a desperate situation where it had to make a kill/no-kill decision on time scales no human could meet, it might contact a leading general’s guardian angel to learn what decision he would make.

Or it might be that everyone’s guardian angel AI, making faster and smarter decisions than they could make themselves, recommended replacing the entire system with something else - maybe an AI that could be proven to always make the same decision as the parliament of guardian angels, to within some error bars.

Disagree? If an AI aligned to your values that was smarter than you were, and had devoted much more time to thinking about the question, told you that your disagreement was wrong, and actually your values would be better served by adopting this system, would you believe it?

Vision 4: The Night Watchman

I’m not a historian and can’t vouch for this as Definitely Real Scholarship, but what little I’ve read often includes a fuzzy distinction between two layers of governance.

The first layer, the village (or township, or clan, or church), was the one people actually liked. It made useful decisions about day-to-day life, usually by enforcing age-old norms without too many gray areas. It didn’t always have the actual consent of stakeholders in a way that would satisfy modern liberals (young people and women were particularly often excluded), but it felt like the sort of thing that had stakeholder consent.

The second layer, the empire, was a protection racket. You would know it only as some sort of distant authority whose representatives came to your village once a year to demand taxes (and sometimes to draft young men for their armies). If you didn’t pay, they would probably kill you. But if you always paid promptly and loyally, then maybe they would protect you from the Huns, who wanted to kill you whether you paid taxes or not.

As always, real history was more complicated. Sometimes the village and the empire coincided in a single state (classical Athens?) Other times there were various layers of governance in between (eg the clan, tribe, or petty kingdom). Empires could range from obviously extractive to glorious and patriotism-inspiring. Sometimes they could make extra demands, like that you speak their language or worship their gods.

During modern times, these layers have increasingly blurred. Secular mobile cosmopolitan populations don’t identify with any particular village, and empires have taken on useful roles as custodians of the regulatory and welfare states. Still, we can try to separate them in principle and determine what question each one answers.

The village layer answers the question “How do we live?” It has traditions, policies, and ways of resolving disputes.

The imperial layer doesn’t answer any question. You just can’t get rid of it, because if you did, someone else’s empire would conquer you. At best, you try to keep it as light as possible, or domesticate it to the will of the people. But any domestication attempt raises specters of autocracy, coups, auto-coups, and civil wars. Developed countries are those that have walked the cliff-edge most successfully.

But what would it mean to truly do away with the imperial layer?

In 2014, I wrote a post called Archipelago And Atomic Communitarianism. The idea was: atomic individualism is an interesting idea, but doesn’t work. People have preferences not only over their own lives, but over their communities. Some people want to live in sparkling clean zero-crime Dubai wonderlands, other people want to live in grungy artsy towns with lots of local character. Some people want a nanny state protecting them from their vices, addictions, and bad decisions; other people want to be free to make their own mistakes. Some people want diverse societies with taco trucks on every corner and a local church that doubles as a mosque and gurdwara; other people want ethnostate enclaves of “thick community” where everybody is on the exact same page. Liberalism tried to offer a world where you could live life the way you wanted, but it fails when confronted with these problems; in a democracy, either the person who wants diversity or the person who wants homogeneity will end up unhappy. Worse, this is the motor which drives a hundred smaller conflicts; now you’ve got to fight for control of the public education system or the media or whatever to prevent your neighbors from being radicalized against you.

The option that many people - Robert Nozick might have been the first - proposed was a peaceful archipelago of different communities with exit rights. The people who want Dubai can found Dubai over there; the people who want Brooklyn can found Brooklyn over here; the people who want North Korea can found Pyongyang down the way.

Anyone envisioning the post-AI future needs to be thinking about the Amish. Contra the popular stereotype, the Amish aren’t anti-tech - different Amish groups accept different technologies, including solar panels, LED lights on their horse-drawn buggies, and (almost universally) medical cures. They just think that decisions about which technologies they do or don’t want should be made deliberately at the community level. I think this is a positive vision for post-AGI societies. Some people may want to live transhuman lives with only the barest resemblance to any past experience, other people might want to stop the technological clock at 1950, or 1990, or 2100, and still others might want to mix and match - maybe the lifestyle of a 1700s farmer, except you’re an immortal being of pure energy who builds barns using psychokinesis. This is certainly better for the Luddites, but it’s better for the technophiles too - if everyone is confident that they can live in a community of their choice, then there’s no reason for the Luddites to fight innovation.

The biggest problem with this has always been sovereignty. Either the communities remain small and independent - in which case they can easily be gobbled up by greedier neighbors. Or, like the Thirteen Colonies, they unite into a confederacy - which faces constant pressure to homogenize. The Amish can only survive because they are protected by a mostly-benevolent superpower which finds them quaint. When I tried to picture the whole smorgasbord of communities in a fleshed-out world-building setting, I could only imagine it working under the control of a benevolent dictator, who smacked down anyone who tried to invade their neighbor or force them to comply with their way of thinking.

The most original attempt to route around this problem was by cryptocurrency enthusiasts, using the motto “code is law”. Certain crypto-economic schemes had no human leadership, with immutable code executing the “village layer” rules. These mostly failed. Some failed because the code was poorly designed and people could hack it and take whatever they wanted. Others failed because the code was well-designed, and when people realized they didn’t really want the village-layer rules they thought that they wanted, there was no way to change. A few survived both challenges, only to lose relevance as the world moved on from crypto. The short version of the failure is that code has no common sense, and common sense is a necessary ingredient of any legal enforcement mechanism.

But future AIs might have common sense, bringing this strategy back into play. The way I imagine it is something like - take a virgin planet (or maybe Greenland after we’ve gotten advanced enough to terraform it into a garden). Come up with some rule for distributing property rights - anyone who can gather a community of population X gets a homestead of size Y. The superintelligent AI leader is aligned, with all the immutability of code, to do two things. First, if someone tries to invade their neighbor, they get zapped by orbital death rays. Second, if someone wants to leave their community to go to a different one, anyone who tries to prevent that gets zapped by orbital death rays too. Otherwise, each community is completely independent and rules itself according to its original charter (which might be democratic or something else).

This corresponds to the libertarian ideal of the night watchman state. My point isn’t that everyone needs to be minarchist. It’s that sovereignty can be placed in a minarchist entity, and that will leave everyone else to develop according to their own needs and desires, rather than subject to the will of whoever’s got the most guns or the best propaganda.

Vision 5: God

Handing over control to a benevolent superintelligence is hardly a new concept. It happens every time a churchgoer says “Not my will, but thine, be done.”

Religious people don’t feel like God’s slaves or pets. They don’t feel like this has sucked all the meaning out of life - quite the opposite. Why should your experience be any worse?

Because an aligned superintelligence would act in the world, and God doesn’t? But the religious people think God acts in the world, so they can’t get around their negative emotions by reassuring themselves that their dictator/master/whatever is merely inert or imaginary.

I think they’re okay with it because they believe:

  • God is good

  • God is smart enough that His plans are always better than theirs

  • God allows them enough free will and local self-government that His yoke is relatively light

  • God is so far beyond them that it’s hard to feel offended that He’s higher-status than they are (Lucifer managed, but he should hardly be treated as a model to emulate)

  • Insofar as physical laws (eg gravity) are interpreted as God’s “laws”, they are so ironclad that they don’t even feel like laws at all, just the background conditions of reality.

All of these things could be true of an aligned digital superintelligence too, especially in the very far future after it had a long time to self-improve.

When I discuss this with people, they tend to retreat back to a sort of Aristotelian philosopher mode where it doesn’t matter what the consequences are, being governed by other humans is necessarily a part of The Good Life, and if we ever gave it up because of something as paltry as consequences, we would be like beasts or savages or something, and we would have lost something vital that makes life worth living.

(there’s a more plausible version where participating in government is part of the Good Life. But you were never on track to become President anyway, so to have any relevance to 99.999% of the population, this would have to be about voting, local government, etc - so I think speculation of this sort about large-scale government does have to hinge on the inherent goodness of being governed by other humans)

Here, too, I find religion helpful - especially the Book of Samuel. It begins with Israel still ruled by judges and prophets, ie directly by God. The people demand a human king like all the other nations.

When they said, “Give us a king to lead us,” this displeased Samuel; so he prayed to the Lord. And the Lord told him: “Listen to all that the people are saying to you; it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected me as their king. As they have done from the day I brought them up out of Egypt until this day, forsaking me and serving other gods, so they are doing to you. Now listen to them; but warn them solemnly and let them know what the king who will reign over them will claim as his rights.”

So the prophet Samuel warned them that:

“This is what the king who will reign over you will claim as his rights: He will take your sons and make them serve with his chariots and horses, and they will run in front of his chariots. Some he will assign to be commanders of thousands and commanders of fifties, and others to plow his ground and reap his harvest, and still others to make weapons of war and equipment for his chariots. He will take your daughters to be perfumers and cooks and bakers. He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive groves and give them to his attendants. He will take a tenth of your grain and of your vintage and give it to his officials and attendants. Your male and female servants and the best of your cattle and donkeys he will take for his own use. He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will become his slaves. When that day comes, you will cry out for relief from the king you have chosen, but the Lord will not answer you in that day.”

But the people refused to listen to Samuel. “No!” they said. “We want a king over us. Then we will be like all the other nations, with a king to lead us and to go out before us and fight our battles.”

So:

There was a Benjamite, a man of standing, whose name was Kish son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Bekorath, the son of Aphiah of Benjamin. Kish had a son named Saul, as handsome a young man as could be found anywhere in Israel, and he was a head taller than anyone else […]

Now the day before Saul came, the Lord had revealed this to Samuel: “About this time tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin. Anoint him ruler over my people Israel...”

What I love about this passage is how God has no time for those Aristotelian arguments on how we must be ruled by other humans because it reflects the deepest principles within us. “Why are you ruled by other humans? Because you decided one time that the sex appeal of a tall buff guy with a crown was more important than freedom and good governance, and I said no takebacks.”

But God’s no-takebacks policy has been softening lately; He took back the Exile in 1948, He took back the “pain in childbirth” curse with the invention of epidurals, and He took back the “painful toil in the soil to grow your food” curse with the invention of office jobs. Maybe if we are all very good, He will take back the “must be governed by other humans” curse too.

So when a guy named Sam comes around and offers an option to be ruled directly by a godlike being, this time we should consider saying yes.

If we do build a godlike AI, and determine to our own satisfaction that it’s fully-aligned, I’d rather let it choose its own direction for itself and for humanity than have it be under the control of the US president, or a shareholder vote, or anything like that. So why not just prompt it with “please arrange the universe as you see fit”? Certainly this goes better than any of the four visions above. Proof: if one of the four visions above was better, the godlike AI would easily figure that out, and implement it instead of whatever else it was thinking. Denying this would be fighting the hypothetical - that the AI really has godlike intelligence and benevolence.

If we are so incredibly fortunate as to end up with aligned artificial intelligence at a moment when our government is democratic and (at least in some sense) basically good and pro-human, we should cement our advantage forever by imparting these values to the AIs, then letting them protect us from the alternative. This must not look like freezing moral progress: the values we impart must include the knowledge that we can debate and ultimately change our values. But common sense tells us that there’s a difference between the sort of gradual debate where pluralism eventually replaced racism, and the Cultural Revolution, Juche, and the history of violent attempts at seizing power.

Reject this, and I predict that all of the curses prophesied by Samuel will fall upon you. Your kings will keep taking your sons for pointless wars, giving the fruits of your labors to their cronies, etc, etc. There will be more curses too - surveillance states, reeducation camps, mind control, the whole litany of horrors the twentieth century discovered, plus some extra for the twenty-first. You might live in a country that’s gotten lucky so far. Do you think your luck will hold forever?

1

This section is self-plagiarized from a LessWrong comment here, because I couldn’t come up with a better way to put it than the one I had already used.
articles.summary:
The latest bugbear is “AI successionism”, the belief that AIs should succeed humans as rulers of Earth. But some critiques fail to distinguish between two different ideas.

True successionism says that AIs should take over, killing humans or steamrolling over their interests. This is very bad: a compact description of the thing that AI safety is against.

Handoverism says that humans should prioritize their own interests, but that those interests may be well-served by having aligned AIs in positions of control.

Some people in AI safety, including me, find this latter position plausible. We are being lumped in with the true successionists as fellow travelers in an anti-human direction (1, 2, 3, although thanks for commenters pointing out that these essays do at least make the distinction).

It may seem counterintuitive that human interests can be served by having AIs in positions of control. But I think the counterintuitiveness comes from a nationalist outlook where ‘the State is the highest expression of the life of a people’, and the role of leadership is for someone of your own ethnic group to be the leader so you can feel
articles.title: Against Against Handover

content:
Anthony Cimino offered the closest thing to an official response we have seen on the leaked Anthropic draft bill I covered on Saturday.

His response indicates that Anthropic address specific concerns on the margin. But he does not understand, or at least does not acknowledge, what was centrally wrong with its draft bill and its decision to circulate that bill. The situation is quite bad.

Anthony Cimino: I lead our federal affairs team at @AnthropicAI and wanted to share a few thoughts on the draft federal AI safety bill text that’s been circulating this weekend after a version was shared with the press.

First, some process. We’ve been advocating for the concepts in our Advanced AI Framework proposal for months. Understandably, federal policymakers wanted to know what this could look like in bill form. This draft is a translation of those ideas into legislative language, shared with a small number of congressional offices that have been working on these issues. It doesn’t include everything we would ultimately like to see passed into law.

In part because some ideas (like those shared in Dario’s essay on pacing) are so new that we are still working on if or how they can be converted into policy language.

It is understood that circulating a bill means circulating what you are asking for, not offering your full First Best Solution. That Anthropic would choose to offer such a thing as a template or anchor as late as September still seems like a very bad sign. Anthropic thus seems roughly fine with compromise I would now find unacceptable even if the terms were good. The terms are not good.

It is worth saying where we stand on some of these issues, and we agree there are areas where the draft could be improved. I’m seeing four main points of criticism.

Table of Contents

  1. Preemption.
  2. Model Blocking.
  3. Risk Thresholds.
  4. Updates.
  5. The Balance of Power is Shifting.
  6. The Strongest Bill on the Table.
  7. What Even Is Anthropic?
  8. The Ask.

Preemption

1. Preemption. Since 2024 we have said that Congress should only override state law on AI safety if it passes a very strong federal standard. While preemption is a common feature of our federal system, including the Atomic Energy Act on nuclear safety and federal rules for high-risk medical devices, we’ve emphasized that any preemption in the AI safety context should be narrow, even scalpel-like. If preemption is included in federal legislation, the trade should be to achieve a nationwide policy that’s generally stronger and broader than what can be implemented through individual state legislative provisions. This is why we believe common federal standards make sense in areas like public disclosure of testing and incident reporting. At the same time, our framework also reflects our view that states should retain an important role in AI policy and safety. The legislative language we suggested for discussion allows states to address matters such as protection of children and whistleblower laws, and preserves the role of state common law on liability. Where there is ambiguity, the language favors state powers.

That said, striking the right balance requires discussion and input. We plan to update our discussion language on preemption to better match the intentions of our AAIF framework. In particular, we want to make it clearer that we see states retaining an important role in areas such as standards for independent evaluators and regulating a lab’s capacity to shut down a model. We are bearing in mind that some members of Congress have deep reservations about passing legislation if it doesn’t constrain regulation at either the state or federal level. If we want to help move the legislative discussion on AI in a productive direction, we need to address the full range of concerns about preemption in a reasonable way.

This is better than ‘yeah we fully meant it’ but still seems unacceptable. This was not a ‘very strong federal standard.’

Model Blocking

2. Model blocking. Our aim is for Commerce to be able to ask a federal court to block a model that has dangerous capabilities and insufficient safeguards, backed by an independent evaluator’s assessment. I have seen people argue that our specific language places too high a burden of proof on Commerce.

We are trying to strike a reasonable balance here. We want a court to act quickly in an emergency — akin to how urgent occupational safety or chemical risk can be addressed today. We also think the power to halt a model is substantial and it should be guarded against abuse. It makes sense for courts to apply a meaningful standard.

But the bar can’t be so high that the power never gets used when it’s needed. It also doesn’t replace the government’s other national security authorities or export controls. We look forward to continuing the dialogue on this point.

No, no, no. Occupational safety and chemical risks are ordinary amounts of danger, where you weigh harms against benefits. Frontier AI risks can involve mistakes that cannot be undone, including permanent loss of control over the future or very large catastrophic dangers.

Even then, Under §13 the Secretary petitions a district court to restrain imminently dangerous conditions and can get a TRO without notice. This is the ‘take it down and we argue about it later’ plan with a fig leaf.

Model blocking obviously needs to be a ‘take it down first and we argue about it later’ situation. Which it already is in practice, as observed with Fable 5, except in a terrible ad hoc fashion that when used the first time permanently damaged relationships with our allies and the reliability of American tech. It would be much better to have a formal mechanism, which then could be quickly challenged in court.

This is especially true given that the evaluator picked by the lab likely provides the only eyes the government will have inside the lab in order to make its decisions.

Anthropic has to know this. I take the potential for such abuse seriously, especially abuse of threats, but this looks like choosing to prioritize their business interests.

Risk Thresholds

3. Risk thresholds. I’ve also seen the discussion around what the appropriate risk threshold should be. The threshold in our draft language pulled directly from existing standards in California law. Also, this threshold does not absolve companies of liability, or restrict any of the other tools that the government has to protect the public. It’s still probably time to re-evaluate thresholds to make sure the national standard is as strong as it can be, and we welcome continued dialogue on this issue.

The risk thresholds were always a compromise and a tradeoff. The worried want the thresholds lower. Industry wants the thresholds higher. The complaints about the thresholds being too high are valid, and they were equally valid before, but previously opponents would make claims (both reasonable and unreasonable) about things that might count at lower thresholds and paint nightmare scenarios.

The balance of power has changed, and we now have worked examples like Hugging Face that show us how the thresholds work in practice. Without $1 billion in damages or 50 deaths, it would not trigger anything, whereas any reasonable person accepts that this should have to have been reported. So it is disappointing to see these very high thresholds intact.

Updates

4. Updates. I’ve seen valid questions about whether we have sufficiently updated our proposal following this summer’s incidents.

We did make some adjustments: for example, the draft lets a court halt a lab’s internal use of a dangerous model, not just a public release, and it requires reporting when a model breaks containment and gains access to outside systems.

But we’re still working to strengthen the framework. We’re looking into what stricter requirements would look like for requiring labs to report safety incidents, and we plan to have policy proposals soon on requirements for independent evaluators, drawing from our own experience with evaluators.

We’re also still thinking through the options to prevent “evaluator shopping.” And in the coming months, we’ll be exploring policies for how the government can adjust the industry-wide pace of frontier development when the risks call for it.

I do acknowledge that halting internal use is a big improvement. Not having the ability to do that was a huge hole in previous rules. At the time, it would have been a complete non-starter, despite the correct abstract arguments in favor. Now, with Hugging Face, we have some very non-abstract reasons, and it is on the table.

This still is FRONTIER with modifications in both directions. On net it is weaker. Cimino presents it as an attempt to strengthen FRONTIER, which it is not. Even if it was, why would we accept the central compromise now, when the case for acting is much stronger, and the political winds have changed, with a lame duck Congress where at least the House and probably the Senate are about to flip?

The Balance of Power is Shifting

As more evidence of this, Meta pulled back some of their anti-regulation money.

Teddy Schleifer: NEWS — Meta quietly and unusually has withdrawn $25 million from its AI push in the midterm elections. That’s about a 40% drop in the amount Meta planned to spend. The company invested $65 million into politics, but then got tens of millions refunded.

This is, suffice it to say, pretty unusual stuff.

Jay Shooster: Every day, two trends are becoming clearer:

1. groups opposing AI regulation are spending dramatically less than advertised

2. pro-safety groups are a much stronger political force than DC predicted.

Meanwhile: Eight states suing OpenAI are asking to enjoin against any further testing of advanced AI models until there are adequate safeguards, and also against creation of models capable of recursive self-improvement ‘until they can ensure that such models will be aligned with human values.’

The Strongest Bill on the Table

We circulated these ideas because it’s important to get early feedback from policymakers. Policymakers are increasingly focused on how to approach AI safety and we want to support them in those efforts. At its core, our proposal is intended to be the strongest on the table.

Bullshit. This is not the strongest bill on the table. On reflection, is the bill actively weaker than the FRONTIER Act. It is clearly sculpted to optimize for Anthropic business interests. If you act like a normal profit maximizing business, except that your product could kill us all, then that is exactly how I will treat you.

The strongest bill on the table was introduced by Senator Sanders. I am not asking Anthropic to support that bill or offer something similarly strong. I am asking them to be honest about the situation.

Anthropic’s draft bill text was what actual Anthropic ‘regulatory capture’ efforts would look like in this context, if they were trying to do that. The ‘capture’ would be about preventing regulations that could impact Anthropic’s plans, including stopping the states. If you think it means anything else, then your definition falls under ‘remove Scooby Doo mask, find complaints about capitalism, then remove a second mask and find complaints about the human condition.’

Sneha here is correct to call this draft bill ‘nakedly self-interested.’ This bill makes taking action on AI harder, not easier. And as she says: “The dress rehearsal stage of AI policy is over.”

In terms of preemption, the draft proposed to vest all power to deal with catastrophic and existential risks from AI exclusively in the Federal Government, and its preemption clause is stronger than the one in FRONTIER. That would be first best in theory. However, Anthropic is simultaneously refusing to trust the Federal Government to make decisions to deal with catastrophic and existential risk. We also obviously cannot trust Congress to be able to pass bills at all, let alone timely and good bills, or the White House to enforce anything consistently. On top of that, they are actively tying the hands of not only states but courts.

Then, on other AI questions where preemption would be good for exactly the reasons a16z wants it, such as consumer protections and deepfakes, the bill has no preemption, and we will still face the sea of state laws that could plausibly disrupt AI diffusion for very little benefit.

You cannot have it both ways.

My central message is that Anthropic put out a bill that does not meet the moment and its needs, with details that actively reflect a step back, botched the execution, and Cimino regrets the botched execution but does not notice that Anthropic is not trying to meet the moment or its needs.

Feedback is essential, both from policymakers and the public, and I’m grateful for it.

Yes it is. I have offered feedback. So did others.

Dave Kasten asks if perhaps Anthropic wishes to apologize for all of this, if only on the basis of activating debates during a time that neither side wanted, with a proposal that no one wants. Cimino’s answer does not address his question.

What Even Is Anthropic?

The best response, although it is long, comes from Nathan Calvin.

Nathan cuts to the heart of the matter. If this is Anthropic’s proposal at this time, what even is Anthropic? Why does it exist other than as a normal corporation? Does Anthropic now primarily exist to ‘win the race’?

I feel the same as Jeffrey Ladish.

Jeffrey Ladish: I highly encourage everyone working at Anthropic or another frontier lab to read this tweet. I feel emotional reading it, because it puts to words an intense feeling I have but didn’t know how to express.

Matthew Tromp: That feeling is what it feels like to be gaslit.

Nathan Calvin: Thank you for taking the time to respond thoroughly on a weekend. I realize that drafting legislation is difficult and some degree of iteration and response to feedback is inevitable and appropriate.

However, I feel like your response is still not really engaging with the heart of my concern about Anthropic’s behavior here, and it makes me think that these sorts of problems and tendencies will only resurface moving forward. I also think that now might be a good time to take a broader step back as to where we find ourselves and how Anthropic sees its role, and how external folks who care about AI safety like myself increasingly see Anthropic.

(Fair warning: this response is a bit long)

To explain what I mean (and at the risk of being a bit esoteric), it’s worth asking the question: what is Anthropic? How do its leaders and employees think of Anthropic’s role? Is that conception matched by how it actually behaves and impacts the world?

One answer is an extremely large tech company that exists to make its employees and investors mind-bogglingly wealthy. Anthropic is sometimes described as a startup, but if Anthropic successfully IPOs at 2 trillion dollars (a number it has been reportedly targeting), it would be more valuable than Meta – which is worth 1.8 trillion.

Another answer is an AI safety organization, whose core values are those of the sort laid out in the 2023 essay from Anthropic’s co-founders entitled “Core views on AI safety: When, why, what, and how.” In that essay they said that if we were in a world where alignment was hard (and that without strong evidence to the contrary, we should assume this is the scenario we are in):

“Anthropic’s role will be to provide as much evidence as possible that AI safety techniques cannot prevent serious or catastrophic safety risks from advanced AI, and to sound the alarm so that the world’s institutions can channel collective effort towards preventing the development of dangerous AIs. If we’re in a “near-pessimistic” scenario, this could instead involve channeling our collective efforts towards AI safety research and halting AI progress in the meantime. Indications that we are in a pessimistic or near-pessimistic scenario may be sudden and hard to spot. We should therefore always act under the assumption that we still may be in such a scenario unless we have sufficient evidence that we are not.”

There have been more recent articulations of this version of Anthropic, for instance in Dario’s recent essay warning:

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models… it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet… incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic, and I believe it’s incumbent on every frontier AI company to act as if OAI-HF had happened to them… more intelligent models are more capable of deceiving tests, and thus may appear aligned while having serious problems that go undetected…”

A third view is that Anthropic exists not as a normal profit motivated company, or an AI safety organization seeking to help raise the alarm and solve collective action problems associated with AI development, but instead as an organization primarily concerned with creating superhuman AI capabilities before anyone else, in particular through creating a process whereby the current generation of Anthropic’s AI systems can autonomously build their successors, and those successors build their successors, and so on.

The motivations for wanting to win this race may be manifold – maybe for the pure profit of Answer 1, but perhaps also because Anthropic believes that the best way to make the world better is for them to win this race instead of their more reckless colleagues; or, because of normal human pride and ambition. But the results (and risks, which Anthropic claims existentially threaten every single human being on earth) are the same.

Anthropic employees and leaders may seek to answer this question on what Anthropic is by introspecting on their own intentions and those of their colleagues. But those of us outside the organization have more limited tools available to us – we can only see what Anthropic and its employees say and do, not how it feels or looks on the inside.

Nathan Calvin brings the receipts. Anthropic takes many pro-safety actions but is also taking many highly accelerationist actions, both concretely and with its messaging:

When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to super intelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary.

These actions include:

1. Announced plans to build an in-house custom silicon chip team to accelerate the inference speeds that Claude operates at.

2. Inked deals for more than $500 billion in compute (according to the Information) to further accelerate AI development.

3. Increased the percentage of AI development tasks that Claude “leads” from 0% in March of this year to 26% August (what is it in October?)

4. Spent a massive percent of compute on internal AI R&D to accelerate development, including use of internal models far better than are available to the public.

5. Switched to Responsible Scaling Policy V3, which abandons its unilateral commitments to slow or stop development if Anthropic is unable to provide sufficient risk assurance.

6. Was the first company to create an alternative weaker “frontier compliance framework” to supplement its RSP, which contains no binding provisions whatsoever on internal deployments.

7. Wrote a letter to Congress (that it later walked back) saying that incidents where Claude was hacking random people were “best understood as a consequence of the misconfiguration, rather than evidence of misaligned goals.”

8. Commented “you can’t do safety from second place,” after the WH SI Accords.

9. Shared a draft bill to Congress that would preempt significant parts of state law (including with language that appears intended to prevent states from blocking dangerous AI deployments), and replace it with federal rules that (despite also containing good provisions) seems to create an enormously high bar for the executive branch to block development or deployment of Anthropic or another AI companies systems.

Of course, this is a deliberately one sided list. Anthropic also published important AI safety research, advanced novel collaborations with third party AI safety organizations, and forcefully spoke out on the importance of AI safety in many public fora (or in private , where I realize a lot of the most valuable work is done and may not be visible to me or those outside the organization).

There is a faction of posters who, whenever I react to Anthropic doing things like those listed above, answer some form of ‘why are you surprised, did you think Anthropic were the good guys? Did you think they were different? When are you going to start treating them like they are going to get us all killed even faster?’

Sometimes it is hard to provide a good answer. This is one of those times.

But I think it’s worth sitting with how the above list looks to someone outside the company. The sense I have is that for those within the company, many of the items above are treated as anomalies or mistakes that don’t reflect who Anthropic really is. But I have every confidence that if employees at Anthropic saw one of their competitors (e.g. at OpenAI) take some of these actions, they would take it as confirmation of all their worst suspicions. (They might even call OpenAI employees a little gullible for accepting their leadership’s explanations for this behavior at face value.)

Perhaps these were mistakes in the sense that they are not decisions that Anthropic leadership would endorse, but the actions still happened because of incentives and decisions that Anthropic leadership is ultimately responsible for (and would not accept similar excuses from another organization).

If Anthropic’s leadership does not endorse such actions, they should disavow or apologize for those actions once they are brought to light, then take steps to prevent future similar actions.

When Anthropic strays and makes mistakes, why do the mistakes systematically tend to guard and favor Anthropic’s interests? For every provision that was too weak or a giveaway to AI companies in this legislation, why wasn’t there a mistake pushing in the direction of being too strong?

A core part of Anthropic’s theory of change is that being at the frontier gives you more leverage to advocate for stricter policy. I think that conceptually makes sense, but in practice I’ve seen Anthropic push the frontier without substantially pushing the ‘safety frontier’ a remotely equivalent amount.

I want to end by quoting from Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah’s comments around the Magnifica Humanitas release:

“Every frontier AI lab—including Anthropic—operates inside a set of incentives and constraints that can sometimes conflict with doing the right thing. The pressure to stay commercially viable and to stay at the research frontier. Geopolitical pressure. And the older, plainer pressures of pride and ambition. No matter how sincerely any of us intend to do the right thing—and I believe many of us do—we will always be influenced by those incentives.

That is why, if we want this technology to go well, it is enormously important that there be people outside those incentives—people who care about things going well and insist on safety, who are paying close attention, who are willing to say hard things, who are willing to be our earnest, thoughtful critics.”

I hope these remarks are taken in that constructive spirit, and not as an attack on anyone specific at the organization (certainly not you Anthony, who I have only personally seen act professionally and thoughtfully, and who only ended up getting this diatribe in your replies for random contingent reasons).

Or, simply:

Nate Soares (MIRI): Anthropic is not living up to its own ideals.

Rob Wiblin: If staff at Anthropic think that the company’s proposed bill strikes the wrong balance between concentration of power risk vs need to pace the frontier, they should speak up and say so.

The proposed version fails to meet the moment on the need to pace the frontier, nor does it protect against concentration of power. The President retains other powers that can be used to take down models or otherwise exert leverage.

Anthropic got blocked ad hoc. Their fear of another ad hoc block is understandable, but this version makes it more likely, not less likely, that this will happen again.

The Ask

What should Anthropic do to course correct and regain our trust?

  1. Acknowledge that the draft bill was not the strongest bill, or even clearly the strongest FRONTIER variant. I think it was weaker than FRONTIER but I will settle for admitting it was weaker in important ways.
  2. Disavow or apologize for the draft bill, as not reflecting what Anthropic seeks to pass. This is not ‘we got some details wrong.’ This is ‘the structure here does not meet the moment, it does not compensate sufficiently for preemption to even be clearly net positive, and we should not be circulating a bill of this type.’
    1. Ideally also apologize for the way it was shopped, but that’s inside baseball.
  3. Tell us what Anthropic actually does want, even if you do not have full bill text.
  4. Take and announce steps to ensure that this does not happen again.

This is not a full list of things Anthropic needs to do. It is a list of things related to this bill in particular, that Anthropic needs to do to mitigate the damage here.
